title: Non-text Content
shortExplanation:
All non-text content — images, icons, charts, audio, CAPTCHAs, and interactive controls — must have a text alternative that serves the same purpose. Purely decorative content should instead be hidden from assistive technologies, for example with an empty alt attribute.

Information locked inside an image or sound is invisible to anyone who cannot see or hear it. A text alternative lets that same information be spoken aloud, rendered as braille, enlarged, or searched.

This helps blind and low-vision screen reader users, braille display users, people on slow connections with images disabled, and voice assistants navigating on a user's behalf.

example.pass: A product photo includes alt="Red canvas high-top sneaker with white rubber sole", and a decorative divider graphic uses alt="" so screen readers skip it.
example.fail: A "Buy now" image button has alt="button1", so a screen reader user has no idea what pressing it will do.

title: Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded)
shortExplanation:
Prerecorded audio-only content (like a podcast) needs a text transcript, and prerecorded video-only content (like a silent animation) needs a transcript or an audio track that describes what happens on screen.

A recording that exists in only one sensory channel is completely unusable by someone who cannot use that channel. The alternative carries the same information through a different sense.

This helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users for audio-only content, blind and low-vision users for video-only content, and anyone in a loud or sound-restricted environment.

example.pass: A podcast episode page includes a complete text transcript directly below the audio player.
example.fail: A silent screen-recording demo of a new feature is published with no transcript and no descriptive audio track.

title: Captions (Prerecorded)
shortExplanation:
Prerecorded videos that contain audio must have synchronized captions that include all dialogue plus meaningful sounds, such as speaker identification, music, and sound effects.

Without captions, every spoken word in a video is lost on someone who cannot hear it — and auto-generated captions full of errors can be just as bad as none.

This helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users, people watching with the sound off, and viewers processing content in a non-native language.

example.pass: A training video ships with accurate, human-reviewed closed captions that identify each speaker and note sounds like [phone rings].
example.fail: A product launch video relies on unedited auto-captions that garble technical terms, with no way to follow the actual script.

title: Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded)
shortExplanation:
Prerecorded videos must offer either an audio description of important visual information or a full text alternative (a descriptive transcript) that covers both what is said and what is shown.

Critical information often appears only on screen — on-screen text, demonstrations, charts, who is doing what. A user who cannot see the video needs that information narrated or written down.

This helps blind and low-vision users, and the descriptive transcript also serves deafblind users reading by braille.

example.pass: A tutorial video links to a descriptive transcript that narrates each on-screen step, like "The presenter opens Settings and selects Display."
example.fail: A how-to video where the presenter says "just click here, then this one" while pointing at the screen, with no description of what was clicked.

title: Info and Relationships
shortExplanation:
Structure and relationships that are conveyed visually — headings, lists, data tables, form labels, grouped fields — must also be expressed in code, using real semantic elements like h1–h6, ul, table with header cells, and label.

Screen readers navigate by structure: jumping between headings, announcing table headers for each cell, speaking the label when a field gets focus. If structure exists only as visual styling, none of that works.

This helps screen reader and braille users, people who apply their own stylesheets or reader modes, and anyone relying on software to interpret the page.

example.pass: A checkout form associates every input with a visible label element, and section titles use real heading tags.
example.fail: Section "headings" are just bold, enlarged paragraph text, so a screen reader user can't jump between sections or perceive the page outline.

title: Meaningful Sequence
shortExplanation:
When the order of content affects its meaning, the reading order in the code must match that intended order — no matter how CSS visually arranges things on screen.

Screen readers and keyboard navigation follow the code order, not the visual layout. If CSS rearranges content, assistive technology users can receive instructions, steps, or answers in a scrambled sequence.

This helps screen reader users, keyboard users, and people using reader modes or text-only views.

example.pass: A three-step signup flow keeps steps 1, 2, and 3 in code order, even though the design displays them side by side in columns.
example.fail: A CSS grid visually pairs questions with answers, but in code order a screen reader hears all the answers before any of the questions.

title: Sensory Characteristics
shortExplanation:
Instructions must not depend only on sensory characteristics like shape, color, size, screen position, orientation, or sound. Always pair them with names or text labels.

"Click the button on the right" is meaningless to someone who can't see the layout — and may become wrong when the page reflows on a small screen or at high zoom.

This helps blind and low-vision users, deafblind users, people listening to a page rather than viewing it, and anyone on a different screen size.

example.pass: "Select Submit (the green button below the form)" — the button is identified by name first, with sensory hints as a bonus.
example.fail: "To continue, click the round icon in the corner" — there is no name, so a screen reader user cannot find the control.

title: Use of Color
shortExplanation:
Color must never be the only way information is conveyed — status, errors, required fields, chart categories, or links need a second indicator like text, icons, underlines, or patterns.

Roughly 1 in 12 men has a color vision deficiency, and screen readers do not announce color at all. Information carried by color alone simply vanishes for these users.

This helps people with color blindness, low vision users, screen reader users, and anyone viewing a screen in bright sunlight or grayscale mode.

example.pass: Invalid form fields get a red border plus an error icon and the message "Phone number must contain 10 digits."
example.fail: A form says "fields marked in red are required" with no asterisk, label, or other non-color indicator.

title: Audio Control
shortExplanation:
If audio plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, users must be able to pause it, stop it, or control its volume independently from the system volume.

Screen readers speak through the same speakers — auto-playing audio literally talks over the only channel a blind user has for operating the page, including their ability to find the stop button.

This helps screen reader users above all, plus people with attention or processing difficulties and anyone in a quiet environment.

example.pass: A site with ambient background music places a visible Pause button at the very top of the page, reachable as the first tab stop.
example.fail: A homepage hero video auto-plays with sound and the mute control only appears on mouse hover, unreachable by keyboard.

title: Captions (Live)
shortExplanation:
Live video that includes audio — webinars, livestreams, virtual events — must provide real-time captions of the spoken content and meaningful sounds.

A live event can't be paused or replayed; without live captions, deaf and hard-of-hearing participants are excluded from the conversation as it happens.

This helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users, people in noisy spaces, and attendees following along in a non-native language.

example.pass: A company all-hands livestream includes professional real-time captioning (CART) displayed in the player.
example.fail: A live product webinar offers no captions, with a promise that "a captioned recording will be posted later."

title: Audio Description (Prerecorded)
shortExplanation:
Prerecorded videos must provide audio description: narration added during pauses in dialogue that describes important visual details like on-screen text, actions, and scene changes. At Level AA, a transcript alone is no longer sufficient — this strengthens 1.2.3.

If information is shown but never spoken, a person who can't see the screen misses it even while hearing everything perfectly.

This helps blind and low-vision users following video content in real time.

example.pass: A demo video offers an alternate audio-described track: "She selects the Reports tab and a bar chart of monthly sales appears."
example.fail: An instructional video shows each step silently while music plays, and the spoken narration never says what is happening on screen.

title: Orientation
shortExplanation:
Content must work in both portrait and landscape orientation. Locking to a single orientation is only allowed when it is essential, like a piano-playing app or a check-deposit camera view.

Many people mount their device in a fixed position — on a wheelchair, an arm mount, or a stand — and physically cannot rotate it to satisfy an app's preferred orientation.

This helps wheelchair users with mounted tablets, people with motor disabilities who can't easily rotate a device, and anyone whose device rotation is locked.

example.pass: A learning app reflows its layout cleanly whether the tablet is held in portrait or landscape.
example.fail: A banking app displays "Please rotate your device" and refuses to function in landscape, blocking a user whose tablet is mounted sideways.

title: Identify Input Purpose
shortExplanation:
Form fields that collect common personal information — name, email, phone, address, credit card — must declare their purpose in code, typically with the HTML autocomplete attribute.

Declared purposes let browsers and assistive tools auto-fill the field or display familiar icons, sparing users from retyping data they struggle to remember or enter.

This helps people with cognitive and memory disabilities, people with motor disabilities for whom typing is slow or painful, and everyone who uses autofill.

example.pass: The email field is coded as input type="email" autocomplete="email", so the browser offers to fill it instantly.
example.fail: A checkout form disables autocomplete on every field, forcing a user with a tremor to hand-type their full name, address, and card number.

title: Contrast (Minimum)
shortExplanation:
Regular text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background; large text (roughly 24px, or 18.5px bold) needs at least 3:1. Logos, disabled controls, and purely decorative text are exempt.

Low-contrast text becomes unreadable long before it becomes invisible — for aging eyes, in bright sunlight, or on a dim screen, pale gray on white simply isn't there.

This helps people with low vision and color vision deficiency, older users, and everyone reading a screen in poor lighting.

example.pass: Body text uses dark gray #595959 on white — a 7:1 ratio, comfortably above the 4.5:1 minimum.
example.fail: Help text is light gray #AAAAAA on white — about 2.3:1, well below the minimum and illegible to many readers.

title: Resize Text
shortExplanation:
Users must be able to enlarge text up to 200% — via browser zoom or text-size settings — without losing any content or functionality: no clipped labels, overlapping lines, or disabled zoom.

Many people with low vision don't use a screen reader; they read by making text bigger. A layout that breaks at 200% takes the content away from exactly the people who need it most.

This helps people with low vision, older users, and anyone who bumps up text size for comfort.

example.pass: At 200% browser zoom, the page reflows: all text remains visible and every menu and button still works.
example.fail: A mobile page sets maximum-scale=1 to block pinch zoom, and at 200% desktop zoom the fixed-height navigation cuts menu labels in half.

title: Images of Text
shortExplanation:
Use real text rather than pictures of text whenever the same visual presentation is possible with fonts and CSS. Exceptions: logos, and cases where the text presentation is essential or user-customizable.

Images of text blur when magnified, ignore user font and spacing preferences, can't be translated or searched, and their contrast can't be adjusted.

This helps people with low vision who zoom, people with dyslexia who apply custom fonts and spacing, and users of translation tools.

example.pass: A promotional banner is built with web fonts and CSS styling, so it stays sharp at any zoom level and can be read aloud.
example.fail: A restaurant publishes its entire menu as a JPEG — blurry at zoom, invisible to screen readers, and untranslatable.

title: Reflow
shortExplanation:
Content must reflow into a single column at a width of 320 CSS pixels — equivalent to 400% zoom on a typical desktop — without requiring scrolling in two directions. Exceptions exist for content that genuinely needs 2D layout, like data tables and maps.

When zoomed content forces horizontal scrolling, reading means dragging back and forth for every single line — exhausting enough that people give up.

This helps people with low vision who rely on high zoom, and benefits every mobile user as a side effect.

example.pass: At 400% zoom an article reflows into one readable column; only vertical scrolling is needed.
example.fail: At 400% zoom the page keeps its desktop layout, so reading each sentence requires scrolling right and then back left.

title: Non-text Contrast
shortExplanation:
Visual information needed to identify UI components and their states — input borders, button boundaries, focus indicators, checkbox states — and meaningful graphics like chart lines and icons must have at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors.

If a text field's border is a whisper-pale gray on white, many users can't tell where the field is, whether a checkbox is checked, or which step of a progress bar is active.

This helps people with low vision and color vision deficiency, and everyone using a low-quality or glare-struck display.

example.pass: Form inputs use a #767676 border on white (4.5:1), and the focus ring is a solid high-contrast outline.
example.fail: A toggle switch shows "on" and "off" as two barely different light grays at about 1.4:1 — its state is indistinguishable.

title: Text Spacing
shortExplanation:
Nothing may break — no clipped, overlapped, or hidden content — when users override text spacing up to: line height 1.5× the font size, paragraph spacing 2×, letter spacing 0.12×, and word spacing 0.16×.

People with dyslexia and low vision often apply custom spacing to make text readable. Containers with rigid fixed heights punish them by cutting off the very text they adjusted.

This helps people with dyslexia, low vision, and other reading-related disabilities who customize how text is displayed.

example.pass: When a user's spacing stylesheet kicks in, cards and buttons grow to fit the taller text and everything stays visible.
example.fail: A button with a hard-coded fixed height clips its own label in half as soon as line height increases to 1.5.

title: Content on Hover or Focus
shortExplanation:
Tooltips and popovers that appear on hover or keyboard focus must be: dismissible (e.g., with Escape) without moving the pointer, hoverable (the pointer can move onto the popup without it vanishing), and persistent (it stays until dismissed or no longer relevant).

Screen magnification users see only a small slice of the page — they must physically move the pointer toward a tooltip to read it. If it vanishes en route, or can't be dismissed when it covers something, the page is unusable.

This helps people using screen magnification, people with low vision, and users with motor disabilities who move the pointer slowly.

example.pass: An info-icon tooltip stays open while the pointer travels onto it, and pressing Escape dismisses it instantly.
example.fail: A tooltip disappears the moment the pointer leaves the icon, and while open it covers the input field with no way to close it.

title: Keyboard
shortExplanation:
Every function of the page must be operable with a keyboard alone — no mouse required, and no dependence on the timing of individual keystrokes. The only exception is input that genuinely depends on the path of movement, like freehand drawing.

The keyboard is the universal input: screen readers, switch devices, sip-and-puff systems, and voice control all ultimately emulate keystrokes. A mouse-only feature is closed to all of them.

This helps blind users, people with motor disabilities, switch and voice-control users, and keyboard power users.

example.pass: A custom dropdown opens with Enter, moves through options with arrow keys, and selects with Enter.
example.fail: An image carousel's next/previous controls respond only to mouse clicks — Tab can never reach them.

title: No Keyboard Trap
shortExplanation:
If keyboard focus can move into a component, it must be able to move back out using standard keys — Tab, Shift+Tab, or Escape. If an unusual exit is required, users must be told how.

A keyboard trap turns the rest of the page into unreachable territory: the user can't proceed, can't go back, and often has to reload and start over.

This helps keyboard-only users, screen reader users, and switch users — anyone who can't simply click somewhere else to escape.

example.pass: A modal dialog holds focus inside while open, but Escape closes it and returns focus to the button that opened it.
example.fail: An embedded third-party widget accepts Tab focus but never releases it — every subsequent Tab cycles inside the widget forever.

title: Character Key Shortcuts
shortExplanation:
Keyboard shortcuts made of a single character (letter, number, punctuation, or symbol) must be able to be turned off, remapped to include a modifier like Ctrl, or restricted to when the relevant component has focus.

Speech-input users dictate words — and every letter they speak can fire a single-key shortcut. A stray "k" shouldn't archive an email or delete an item.

This helps speech-input users most, plus people with motor disabilities prone to accidental keystrokes.

example.pass: An email app's single-key shortcuts (e to archive) can be disabled or remapped in settings.
example.fail: Pressing "k" anywhere on the page permanently deletes the selected item, and there is no way to turn the shortcut off.

title: Timing Adjustable
shortExplanation:
For every time limit, users must be able to turn it off, adjust it to at least 10 times the default, or extend it — with at least a 20-second warning and a simple action like pressing a key, repeatable at least 10 times. Exceptions: real-time events, limits over 20 hours, and limits that are truly essential.

People read, type, and navigate at enormously different speeds. A timeout calibrated for an average user silently discards the work of everyone slower.

This helps people with cognitive and motor disabilities, screen reader users working through long forms, and anyone who gets interrupted.

example.pass: Twenty seconds before session timeout, a dialog appears: "Still there? Press Continue to extend your session."
example.fail: A government benefits form silently logs the user out after 10 minutes, erasing 9 minutes of carefully entered answers.

title: Pause, Stop, Hide
shortExplanation:
Any moving, blinking, or scrolling content that starts automatically and lasts more than 5 seconds — and any auto-updating content — must come with a way to pause, stop, or hide it.

Motion on screen is magnetic: for people with attention or cognitive disabilities it can make reading the surrounding content literally impossible, and auto-updates can yank a screen reader's position mid-sentence.

This helps people with ADHD and cognitive disabilities, people with vestibular disorders, low-vision users, and screen reader users.

example.pass: A stock ticker and a news carousel each include a clearly visible pause button.
example.fail: A hero carousel auto-rotates every 4 seconds indefinitely, with no pause control — users can never finish reading a slide.

title: Three Flashes or Below Threshold
shortExplanation:
Nothing on the page may flash more than three times in any one-second period, unless the flashing area is small enough and dim enough to fall below the defined general and red flash thresholds.

Rapid flashing can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy within seconds — this is one of the few WCAG rules where a violation can cause direct physical harm.

This protects people with photosensitive epilepsy and also helps people with migraine and sensory-processing sensitivities.

example.pass: An alert animation pulses twice to draw attention, then remains solid.
example.fail: A "FLASH SALE" banner strobes white-to-red five times per second across the full width of the page.

title: Bypass Blocks
shortExplanation:
Provide a way to skip past content that repeats on every page — most commonly a "Skip to main content" link, supported by proper landmarks and headings.

Without one, a keyboard user must tab through the entire header and navigation — sometimes dozens of stops — on every single page before reaching what they came for.

This helps keyboard-only users, screen reader users, and switch users for whom each keypress costs real effort.

example.pass: The first press of Tab reveals a "Skip to main content" link that jumps focus straight past the navigation.
example.fail: Every page begins with 40 navigation links and no skip link or landmarks, so reaching the content takes 40+ keypresses each time.

title: Page Titled
shortExplanation:
Every page needs a title that describes its topic or purpose, with the distinctive part first — "Order History – Acme Store" rather than "Acme Store" on every page.

The title is the very first thing a screen reader announces when a page loads, and it's what identifies tabs, bookmarks, and search results.

This helps screen reader users confirming they landed in the right place, people with cognitive disabilities, and anyone juggling many browser tabs.

example.pass: The search results page is titled "Search results for 'sneakers' – ShopCo".
example.fail: Every page on the site is titled simply "Home", so all open tabs look identical and screen readers announce nothing useful.

title: Focus Order
shortExplanation:
When tabbing through a page, focus must move in an order that preserves the page's meaning and operability — usually matching the visual reading order. Dialogs receive focus when opened, and focus returns sensibly when they close.

If focus leaps unpredictably — from a form field to the footer and back — keyboard users lose their place, skip required fields, and make errors they can't trace.

This helps keyboard-only users, screen reader users, and low-vision users who need focus to stay where they're looking.

example.pass: Tabbing through a checkout form moves logically: name, address, payment fields, then the Submit button.
example.fail: Stray positive tabindex values make focus jump from the first field to the newsletter signup in the footer, then back up to field two.

title: Link Purpose (In Context)
shortExplanation:
The purpose of every link must be clear from its link text alone, or from the text combined with its programmatic context — the surrounding sentence, list item, or table row.

Screen reader users often pull up a list of all links on a page and navigate from it. A list reading "click here, click here, learn more, learn more" conveys nothing.

This helps screen reader users navigating by links, people with cognitive disabilities, and anyone scanning a page quickly.

example.pass: A link reads "Read our full refund policy" — its destination is obvious even out of context.
example.fail: Three product cards each end with an identical "Learn more" link, indistinguishable in a screen reader's link list.

title: Pointer Gestures
shortExplanation:
Any function operated by a multipoint gesture (like two-finger pinch) or a path-based gesture (like swiping or dragging along a path) must also work with simple single-pointer actions — taps or clicks — unless the gesture is essential.

Precise gestures are out of reach for many people using head pointers, mouth sticks, eye-gaze systems, or hands affected by tremor.

This helps people with motor disabilities and users of alternative pointing devices.

example.pass: A map can be zoomed by pinching or by tapping dedicated + and − buttons.
example.fail: An image gallery can only be browsed by swiping — there are no next/previous buttons.

title: Pointer Cancellation
shortExplanation:
Single-pointer actions must be cancellable: trigger on the up-event (release) rather than the down-event (press), or provide a way to abort or undo. Pressing down on a key of an on-screen piano is the classic essential exception.

Firing on release lets a user who pressed the wrong thing slide their finger or pointer off the control and let go safely — a built-in undo for every accidental touch.

This helps people with tremors and motor disabilities, and everyone who has ever fat-fingered the wrong button.

example.pass: A Delete button activates on release, so pressing it by mistake can be cancelled by sliding off before letting go.
example.fail: A one-click purchase button fires the instant it's pressed down — an accidental touch completes the order with no escape.

title: Label in Name
shortExplanation:
When a control has a visible text label, its accessible name (what assistive technology hears) must contain that visible text — ideally starting with it.

Voice-control users operate the page by saying what they see: "Click Search." If the button visibly says Search but its aria-label says "Submit query form," the spoken command fails and the user is stuck.

This helps speech-input users primarily, and keeps what screen readers announce consistent with what sighted helpers see.

example.pass: A button displays "Search" and its accessible name is exactly "Search" — saying "Click Search" works.
example.fail: A button displays "Send" but is coded with aria-label="Submit message form", so the voice command "Click Send" does nothing.

title: Motion Actuation
shortExplanation:
Features triggered by moving the device (shake to undo, tilt to scroll) or by user motion sensed by a camera must also be operable through ordinary UI controls, and the motion trigger must be disableable — unless motion is essential to the function.

People with tremors trigger shake gestures constantly by accident, while people with limited movement — or devices fixed to a mount — may be unable to perform them at all.

This helps people with motor disabilities and tremors, and anyone whose device is mounted.

example.pass: Shake-to-undo exists, but an Undo button is always available and the shake gesture can be turned off in settings.
example.fail: Shaking the phone is the only way to undo typing, with no button alternative and no way to disable the gesture.

title: Multiple Ways
shortExplanation:
Offer at least two different ways to find any page on the site — for example navigation menus plus a search box, a site map, or a table of contents. Pages that are steps in a process (like checkout) are exempt.

People navigate differently: some browse menus, some search, some scan a site map. A page reachable only through one specific click path is effectively hidden from everyone who navigates another way.

This helps people with cognitive disabilities, low-vision and screen reader users who find one method easier, and frankly everyone.

example.pass: A documentation site offers hierarchical navigation, full-text search, and an A–Z index.
example.fail: Support articles can only be reached by drilling down a single specific menu path — there's no search and no index.

title: Headings and Labels
shortExplanation:
Headings and labels must actually describe the topic or purpose of what they head or label. (Whether headings exist at all is covered elsewhere — this rule is about their quality.)

Screen reader users navigate by jumping between headings, and all users scan them to find content. Vague labels like "Details" or "Section 2" turn navigation into guesswork.

This helps screen reader users navigating by headings, people with cognitive disabilities, and anyone scanning a long page.

example.pass: A settings page uses headings like "Email notifications" and "Privacy controls" — each section's purpose is obvious.
example.fail: A multi-part form labels its sections "Step 1", "Step 2", and "More info", revealing nothing about what each step asks for.

title: Focus Visible
shortExplanation:
Whenever a control has keyboard focus, there must be a visible indicator showing it — typically a focus ring or outline. Removing the browser's default outline without providing a replacement is the classic violation.

A keyboard user without a visible focus indicator is flying blind: they cannot tell which of 50 controls will activate when they press Enter.

This helps keyboard-only users, people with low vision, people with motor disabilities, and users with attention or memory limitations.

example.pass: Every interactive element shows a thick, high-contrast focus ring when reached by keyboard.
example.fail: A global CSS rule sets outline: none for aesthetics, leaving keyboard users with no clue where focus is.

title: Focus Not Obscured (Minimum)
shortExplanation:
When an element receives keyboard focus, it must not be completely hidden behind author-created content like sticky headers, cookie banners, or chat widgets. (At least part of it must remain visible.)

A visible focus indicator is useless if the focused element itself is buried under a floating overlay — the keyboard user is interacting with something they literally cannot see.

This helps keyboard-only users and people with low vision, especially on pages with sticky regions.

example.pass: The page uses scroll-padding so that elements focused near the top scroll into view below the sticky header.
example.fail: Tabbing to footer links leaves them entirely hidden beneath a full-width cookie consent banner.

title: Dragging Movements
shortExplanation:
Anything operated by dragging — reordering lists, sliders, drag-and-drop uploads, kanban cards — must also work through simple single-pointer actions like clicks or taps, unless dragging is essential.

A drag requires pressing, holding, moving precisely, and releasing in one continuous motion — a sequence many people with tremors, limited dexterity, or eye-gaze pointers cannot perform reliably.

This helps people with motor disabilities and users of alternative input devices like head pointers and eye-gaze systems.

example.pass: Kanban cards can be dragged between columns, or moved via a "Move to…" menu on each card.
example.fail: Reordering a playlist works only by dragging rows — there are no up/down buttons or move commands.

title: Target Size (Minimum)
shortExplanation:
Clickable targets must be at least 24×24 CSS pixels, or have enough empty space around them that a 24px circle centered on each target doesn't overlap a neighbor. Inline links in text, native browser controls, and essential sizes are exempt.

Tiny, tightly packed targets cause constant mis-taps for anyone whose pointing is less than surgical — and the consequences range from annoying to destructive (tapping Delete instead of Edit).

This helps people with tremors and motor disabilities, older users, and every mobile user with average-sized thumbs.

example.pass: Toolbar icon buttons are 32×32 pixels with comfortable spacing between them.
example.fail: A row of 16×16 pixel edit/delete/share icons sits flush together, making accidental deletes routine.

title: Language of Page
shortExplanation:
Every page must declare its default human language in code — in HTML, the lang attribute on the html element, like <html lang="en">.

Screen readers choose pronunciation rules from this attribute. A French page without lang="fr" gets read with English pronunciation — turning fluent French into incomprehensible noise. It also drives translation tools and hyphenation.

This helps screen reader users above all, plus users of automatic translation and people using browser reading tools.

example.pass: A Spanish-language page is coded <html lang="es">, so screen readers switch to Spanish pronunciation automatically.
example.fail: A German page omits the lang attribute, so screen readers mangle every word with English pronunciation rules.

title: On Focus
shortExplanation:
Simply moving keyboard focus onto a component must never trigger a change of context — no new windows, no form submission, no jumping focus elsewhere, no navigating to a new page.

Keyboard and screen reader users move focus across everything as their way of exploring the page. If merely landing on a control detonates an action, exploration becomes a minefield.

This helps screen reader users, keyboard-only users, and people with cognitive disabilities who are disoriented by surprises.

example.pass: Tabbing across all the controls in a navigation menu only highlights them — nothing activates until Enter is pressed.
example.fail: When focus lands on the "Help" link, a popup window opens immediately, hijacking the user mid-navigation.

title: On Input
shortExplanation:
Changing a form control's value — picking a select option, ticking a checkbox, typing in a field — must not automatically cause a change of context unless the user has been told beforehand that it will.

Users expect to set a value and then act. A dropdown that navigates the instant an option is highlighted breaks keyboard users completely: they can never arrow past the first option.

This helps keyboard and screen reader users, and people with cognitive disabilities who lose their bearings when pages change unexpectedly.

example.pass: Choosing a country in a select updates nothing until the user presses the adjacent "Apply" button.
example.fail: A "Sort by" dropdown reloads the page the moment a value changes, so arrowing through options fires three page loads.

title: Consistent Help
shortExplanation:
If help mechanisms — contact details, a human contact method, a self-help option, or a chat widget — appear on multiple pages, they must appear in the same relative place and order on every page.

The people most likely to need help are the least equipped to hunt for it. Help that moves around the layout from page to page effectively disappears. New in WCAG 2.2.

This helps people with cognitive and memory disabilities, and anyone who is already stuck and frustrated.

example.pass: The "Chat with us" button sits in the bottom-right corner of every single page.
example.fail: The support link lives in the header on the homepage, the sidebar on product pages, and the footer at checkout.

title: Error Identification
shortExplanation:
When an input error is automatically detected, the item in error must be identified and the error described to the user in text — not just with color, an icon, or a vague failure state.

A red border is invisible to a blind user and ambiguous to a color-blind one. Users need to know which field failed and what exactly is wrong with it.

This helps screen reader users, people with color vision deficiency, and people with cognitive disabilities working through forms.

example.pass: Beside the field: "Email address must include an @ symbol" — visible, specific, and announced to screen readers.
example.fail: Submitting the form just turns two fields red, leaving the user to guess which rule each one broke.

title: Labels or Instructions
shortExplanation:
Wherever the user must enter something, provide labels or instructions: visible field labels, required-field indicators, and format hints like (MM/DD/YYYY) — before the user gets it wrong.

Placeholder text is not a label: it vanishes the moment typing starts, has poor contrast, and leaves users mid-form staring at filled boxes with no reminder of what they were for.

This helps people with cognitive and memory disabilities, screen reader users, and people with motor disabilities for whom every error costs effort to fix.

example.pass: Each field has a permanent visible label, required fields are marked, and the date field's label includes its expected format.
example.fail: A form uses placeholder-only hints that disappear on typing, so reviewing your answers means guessing which box was which.

title: Redundant Entry
shortExplanation:
Information the user already entered earlier in the same process must be auto-populated or available to select — not demanded again. Exceptions: re-entry that is essential, needed for security (like confirming a password), or when the earlier information is no longer valid. New in WCAG 2.2.

Re-typing taxes memory and motor effort, and every repeated entry is another chance for a mismatch error.

This helps people with cognitive and memory disabilities, and people with motor disabilities for whom typing is costly.

example.pass: The payment step offers a "Billing address same as shipping" checkbox that copies everything over.
example.fail: After entering their full address at shipping, the user must type the identical address again from scratch at billing.

title: Language of Parts
shortExplanation:
When a passage or phrase is in a different language than the page, mark it in code with its own lang attribute. Proper names, technical terms, and words that have become part of the surrounding language don't need marking.

Screen readers switch pronunciation per element: a French quotation inside an English page is only intelligible if the quote itself carries lang="fr".

This helps screen reader users reading multilingual content, and improves automatic translation and dictionary lookup.

example.pass: An English article wraps a quoted French proverb in <blockquote lang="fr">, so it is pronounced as French.
example.fail: The same proverb without the attribute is read with English pronunciation, producing meaningless sounds.

title: Consistent Navigation
shortExplanation:
Navigation mechanisms that repeat across pages — menus, search boxes, breadcrumbs — must appear in the same relative order on every page. Items can be added or removed, but the ordering of what remains must hold steady.

Users build muscle memory and mental maps: "Products is the third item." Shuffling navigation forces them to relearn the site on every page.

This helps people with cognitive and memory disabilities, low-vision users who memorize layouts, and screen reader users who rely on a predictable order.

example.pass: The header menu reads Home, Products, Pricing, Support in that order on every page of the site.
example.fail: On some pages Support comes first and Products last, so users must re-scan the whole menu every time.

title: Consistent Identification
shortExplanation:
Components that do the same thing across the site must be identified the same way — same label, same icon, same accessible name. Don't call it "Search" on one page and "Find" on another.

Consistent naming lets users transfer what they learned on one page to every other page; inconsistency makes one feature look like several different ones.

This helps people with cognitive disabilities, screen reader users listening for a known label, and everyone's general sanity.

example.pass: The download action uses the same icon and the label "Download" everywhere it appears.
example.fail: The identical save-to-PDF feature is labeled "Download" on one page, "Export" on another, and "Save" on a third.

title: Error Suggestion
shortExplanation:
When an input error is detected and possible corrections are known, suggest them to the user — unless doing so would compromise security or the purpose of the content (like a quiz answer).

"Invalid input" without guidance strands users at the exact moment they need help; telling them what valid input looks like turns a dead end into a quick fix.

This helps people with cognitive and learning disabilities, low-vision users, and anyone filling out an unfamiliar form.

example.pass: "We couldn't find that state. Did you mean: Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin?" with the expected format shown.
example.fail: The date field rejects "3/4/26" with only the message "Invalid date" — no hint that it wants MM/DD/YYYY.

title: Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data)
shortExplanation:
For pages that create legal commitments, execute financial transactions, or modify/delete stored data, at least one must hold: the action is reversible, the input is checked for errors with a chance to correct, or the user can review and confirm before final submission.

Everyone makes entry mistakes; here a mistake costs money, data, or legal standing. One typo in a transfer amount shouldn't be unrecoverable.

This helps people with cognitive and motor disabilities who make more accidental inputs, and protects every user from high-stakes slips.

example.pass: Checkout ends with a review page summarizing the order, with edit links, before the final "Place order" button.
example.fail: A single click on "Delete account" immediately and permanently erases everything — no confirmation, no undo window.

title: Accessible Authentication (Minimum)
shortExplanation:
Logging in must not require a cognitive function test — memorizing a password, solving a puzzle, or transcribing characters — unless there's an alternative method, a mechanism to assist (like allowing paste and password managers), or the test is object recognition or identifying the user's own content. New in WCAG 2.2.

Blocking paste or banning password managers turns login into a memory exam that locks out people who literally cannot memorize strings.

This helps people with cognitive disabilities, memory impairments, and dyslexia — and makes login easier for everyone.

example.pass: The login form accepts pasted passwords, works with password managers, and offers an emailed magic-link alternative.
example.fail: Login blocks paste "for security," forces the password to be typed from memory, then demands typing distorted CAPTCHA characters.

title: Parsing (Obsolete and removed)
shortExplanation:
This criterion originally required well-formed markup: complete start and end tags, no duplicate IDs, and proper nesting. It was removed in WCAG 2.2 because modern browsers and assistive technologies handle parsing errors automatically.

It still matters historically: audits against WCAG 2.0/2.1 reference it, and the real-world problems it caught — like duplicate IDs breaking label associations — now fail under other criteria such as 1.3.1 and 4.1.2.

Knowing its status helps auditors and practitioners explain why it appears in older reports but no longer applies in WCAG 2.2.

example.pass: An auditor notes 4.1.1 as "not applicable" in a WCAG 2.2 audit and files duplicate-ID issues under 4.1.2 instead.
example.fail: A 2.2 audit report cites a page as failing 4.1.1 for unclosed tags — a criterion that no longer exists in 2.2.

title: Name, Role, Value
shortExplanation:
Every UI component must expose its accessible name, its role (button, checkbox, tab…), and its current states and values to assistive technology — and notify it when they change. Native HTML elements do this for free; custom widgets need ARIA to fill the gap.

A "button" built from a styled div is, to a screen reader, just silence: no name, no role, no way to know it's pressable. This criterion is where most custom-widget accessibility failures land.

This helps screen reader users, voice-control users (who target controls by name and role), and switch users.

example.pass: A custom toggle uses role="switch", aria-checked, and a clear label, so a screen reader announces "Dark mode, switch, on."
example.fail: The menu opener is a clickable div with an icon — no role, no name — so assistive tech presents it as inert text, if at all.

title: Status Messages
shortExplanation:
Status messages — "Item added to cart," "3 results found," "Saving…," form success banners — must be exposed to assistive technology so they're announced without receiving keyboard focus, typically via role="status" or aria-live regions.

Sighted users see these messages appear at a glance; without a live region, a screen reader user hears nothing and has no idea their action did anything.

This helps screen reader users, who otherwise must hunt around the page after every action to discover what changed.

example.pass: "Item added to cart" renders inside a role="status" region, so screen readers announce it while focus stays put.
example.fail: After clicking Save, a small "Saved!" note appears visually but is never announced — the screen reader user clicks Save again and again.
